citation.title: Changing Climates of Conflict: A Social Network Experiment in 56 Schools

standing_assumptions:
The article (PNAS 113(3):566–571; printed pp. 566–571 are main PDF pp. 1–6) and its SI Appendix (43 pages; the printed page number equals the supplement PDF page number) state no theorem, proposition or lemma and give no proof. Their formal objects are the school-level regressions (SI Eqs. (1)–(6)), the exposure mapping, the exposure probabilities and the inverse-probability-weighted regression estimator (SI pp. 16–19), one sentence of asymptotic justification (SI p. 19) and the notes to Tables S6 and S7. There are two official corrections: PNAS 115(15):E3598 (2018), which replaces 30% by 25%, and a 2019 correction that adds a grant number. Everything quoted below was read from the rendered page images.
(S1) Schools and blocks. SI p. 5 (Study design): “Prior to randomization, schools agreed to participate in all measurement aspects of the program, with a 50% chance of receiving the anti-conflict program (the treatment).” “Schools were assigned to blocks of four, and randomized to receive the treatment or not within these blocks.” “Four schools dropped out from the study before the point of randomization, which left the total sample at 56 schools and 24,191 students.” Fig. S1, caption (SI p. 24): “The 56 schools were first blocked into groups of four by pretreatment school level variables including size and student demographics (see SI). Within each of the 14 school blocks, two schools were assigned to control (the two school networks on the left), and two to treatment, the anti-conflict intervention (the two school networks on the right). The nodes depict the population of students at the school. Grey nodes are the “seed eligible” students, selected by a deterministic algorithm and comprising a representative sample of the school. Seed eligibles were blocked into four equally sized groups based on pretreatment characteristics including gender and grade, and half of the students in each block were randomly assigned to be treated (part of the anti-conflict program) if they were in a treatment school; dark green nodes are treated seed eligibles. Nodes in the shape of stars are the social referents, who are in the top 10% of their school in connections reported by other students in the pre-randomization survey.”
(S2) Seed-eligibles and seeds. SI p. 6, with $a_i$ a student's indegree and $b_i$ the student's closure: “The students in each of the gender-grade-$b_i$ blocks with the largest values of $a_i$ were considered eligible for randomization into the seed group, such that we had no fewer than 40 seed-eligible students (schools with fewer than 200 students), and no more than 64 seed-eligible students (schools with less than 550 students). For schools with between 200 and 550, we scaled linearly between 40 and 64 seed-eligible students, rounding to the nearest 4. Table S2 demonstrates the covariate profiles of eligible and ineligible students. All of our estimates are computed conditional on the composition of the seed-eligible groups. Among treated schools, half of the seed-eligibles were block-randomized into the seed group, using 4 blocks constructed using gender, grade, and $b_i$ (using an R package, blockTools).” Main p. 567 (PDF p. 2): “In the 28 of 56 schools randomly assigned to receive the intervention, we selected a group of students (the seed-eligibles) using a deterministic algorithm (see SI Appendix for materials and methods used) designed to represent 15% of the school population, blocked by gender and grade and capped at 64 students (grades ranged from 5 to 8) (SI Appendix, Figs. S1 and S2, and Table S1). We randomly assigned 50% of that group (the seeds) to be invited to participate in the anticonflict intervention, which our team implemented over the course of the school year. Within each seed group at each school (on average 26 seeds at each school, for a total of 728 seeds across 28 schools), a random proportion were social referent seeds, meaning they were in the top 10% of their school in the number of connections reported by other students (i.e., indegree).”
(S3) School-level (climate) regressions. SI p. 13: “We fit the following linear regression model: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + u_{ij}$ (1) where $ij$ denotes the $i$th school in the $j$th block. $Y_{ij}$ denotes school-level outcomes, $\alpha_j$ is a block-level fixed effect, $D_{ij}$ is the school-level treatment assignment, $C_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed group (percentage of seed group that is classified as a social referent), and $C^E_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed eligible group (percentage of seed eligible group that is classified as a social referent). $\tau$ here is the average causal effect of treatment. We include $C^E_{ij}$ as a covariate control here so as to maximize comparability with the interaction model in (4). In all cases, the model is fit with OLS regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors to characterize uncertainty.” The interaction model, Eq. (2) (repeated as Eq. (4)), and its interpretation are transcribed in P037-T14. SI p. 16: “This amounts to fitting the following model for main effects: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + \boldsymbol{\theta}\mathbf{X}_{ij} + u_{ij}$, (5) where $\mathbf{X}_{ij}$ is a vector of school-specific pretreatment covariates (percentage white, percentage English-speaking, average house quality and, where available, pretreatment measurement of $Y_{ij}$).” Main p. 568 (PDF p. 3): “We computed confidence intervals and P values using robust SEs under a normal approximation.” Main p. 567: “(Administrative data were available for 49 of the 56 schools, and we restricted our attention to these schools for analyses of conflict-related events.)”
(S4) Scale of composition. In the targets $C_{ij}$ and $C^E_{ij}$ are fractions in $[0,1]$ (0.20 means 20%), the scale of Fig. 2 and Table S7. The SI's wording (“percentage”, “$c\%$”, “percentage points”) does not match that scale; this is finding P037-N020, rated a clarity note, and is not a target.
(S5) Social-influence setting. SI pp. 16–17: “We have a finite population of students indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$ on which our randomized experiment is performed. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denotes whether or not student $i$ is assigned to be a seed (i.e., is invited to participate in the anti-conflict group). An experimental design is a plan for randomly selecting a particular value of $\mathbf{z}$ with predetermined probability $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Restricting our attention only to treatment assignments that can be generated by our experimental design, define $\Omega = \{\mathbf{z} : p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0\}$, so that $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, ..., Z_N)'$ is a random vector with support $\Omega$ and $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$. In this setting, treatment assignment is the random assignment of seeds both across and within schools according our hierarchical randomization (i.e., so that half of schools are assigned to control schools with no seeds).” The exposure mapping $f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i)$ with $\theta_i$, $\gamma$ and $s_i$ (SI p. 17) is transcribed in P037-T7. SI p. 18: “We allow for each student $i$ to have a vector of potential outcomes, which we denote by $(y_i(d_C), ...y_i(d_D))$, that do not depend on the value of $\mathbf{Z}$. We seek estimates for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$ (i.e., control exposure, school exposure, non-social referent peer exposure, social referent peer exposure) of the average potential outcome $\mu(d_k) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)$.” “$\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\Omega} \mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$.” “We restrict ourselves to the subpopulation of students (n=2451) for which there exists some probability that students could receive all four exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$.” The estimator $\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k)$ (SI p. 19) is transcribed in P037-T11.
(S6) None of the eleven headline claims (P037-H1 to P037-H11) is a mathematical statement: each is an empirical estimate, a description of the design or an interpretive conclusion. Every target below therefore comes from a confirmed error.
(S7) [Added on 6 October 2026, after the authors' analysis code became available; it applies to the revised P037-T2 and to P037-T18 onward.] The authors' eleven R scripts, as released by ICPSR with study 37070, were not available when (S1)–(S6) and P037-T1 to T17 were written. In the targets added or revised afterwards, ‘the released code’ means those scripts as read and run by the checkers; a statement of what the code does is established by the code and is not a statement of the publication. ‘On the public data’ means a value obtained from the public data release (ICPSR 37070 V2) run through the authors' scripts with an adapter, or from a reconstruction on that release; the authors' own analysis files are not public and ICPSR states that some variables in the release were changed, so such a value is not the value the authors would obtain from their own files. No such value is part of a target's statement: the statements are exact identities, probabilities, counts and counterexamples, and values on the public data appear only in notes, as aggregates (the data are respondent-level records of school students; no respondent row and no school identifier is given). The scripts are cited by number: script 1, ‘1. Sanitize and generate perms, probs.R’ (the network, referent status, the simulated seed and school assignments, the exposure indicators and their simulated probabilities); script 2, ‘2. Cleaning.R’ (outcomes and covariates); script 3, ‘3. Network results.R’ (the social-influence estimates and their randomization standard errors); script 4, ‘4. School results-with-correction.R’ (the school-level regressions, their three kinds of standard error, the percentages of the 2018 Correction and Fig. 2); script 6, ‘6. Bond et al analysis.R’ (Fig. S5). Line numbers are those of the released files, as cited by the checkers.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Abstract, Significance statement, Results (first paragraph) and Discussion: the ‘30%’ reduction in disciplinary reports, corrected to 25% (2018 Correction)
canonical_claim.location: main p. 566 (PDF p. 1), p. 569 (PDF p. 4) and p. 571 (PDF p. 6); 2018 Correction, p. E3598 (correction PDF p. 1)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] The four passages are transcribed in P037-T17 and the 2018 Correction in P037-T15. [Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-N001), verbatim] “Replace 30% with 25% in Abstract, Significance, Results page 569, and Discussion page 571 as the official correction directs. Make Results self-contained by labeling 0.20 as the rounded unadjusted control mean and -0.06 as the rounded adjusted effect, and explaining that 25% uses unrounded adjusted quantities for both effect and baseline. This avoids implying the false equality 0.06/0.20 = 25%.”
[Mathematical content.] The Discussion (p. 571) gives the estimated totals of disciplinary events for the 11,938 students in treatment schools: 2,695 without the intervention and 2,012 with it.
(i) $2695 - 2012 = 683$, and the relative reduction implied by the totals is $\dfrac{2695 - 2012}{2695} = \dfrac{683}{2695}$.
(ii) $\tfrac{49}{200} < \tfrac{683}{2695} < \tfrac{51}{200}$, so the reduction is 25% to the nearest whole percent. It is not 30%: $\tfrac{683}{2695} < \tfrac{59}{200}$, and $\tfrac{683}{2695} = \tfrac3{10}$ would require $10\cdot683 = 3\cdot2695$, whereas $6830 \ne 8085$.
(iii) [Rounding of the totals cannot account for 30%.] If $A \in [2694.5, 2695.5]$ and $B \in [2011.5, 2012.5]$, then $\tfrac{1364}{5389} \le 1 - \tfrac BA \le \tfrac{1368}{5391}$, and both bounds lie strictly between $\tfrac{49}{200}$ and $\tfrac{51}{200}$.
(iv) [Consistency with the printed decrease.] $\tfrac{683}{11938}$ lies in $[\tfrac{11}{200}, \tfrac{13}{200})$, so the decrease per student implied by the totals is $0.06$ to two decimals, the printed value; the control level implied by the totals is $\tfrac{2695}{11938}$, which lies in $(\tfrac{9}{40}, \tfrac{23}{100})$ and so is not the printed $0.20$.
(v) [The original calculation.] $\tfrac{0.06}{0.20} = \tfrac{3/50}{1/5} = \tfrac3{10}$ exactly, so the printed 30% is the ratio of the two rounded printed numbers; and no pair $(e, m)$ with $e \in [0.055, 0.065]$ and $m \in [0.195, 0.205]$ has $e/m$ equal to 25% to the nearest whole percent, because $e/m \ge \tfrac{0.055}{0.205} = \tfrac{11}{41} > \tfrac{51}{200}$. The corrected 25% therefore uses a control mean other than the printed $0.20$ (the Correction: both estimates covariate-adjusted).
(vi) $\tfrac3{10} - \tfrac14 = \tfrac1{20}$, which is one sixth of $\tfrac3{10}$: the correction lowers the reported reduction by five percentage points, one sixth of its original size.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The quantities are the paper's: the control-school mean ‘0.20 times per year’ and the ‘average decrease of 0.06 disciplinary events per student in treatment schools’ (Results, p. 569); the estimated totals 2,695 and 2,012 for ‘the 11,938 students in treatment schools’ (Discussion, p. 571); Table S6, Peer conflict, School level main effect $-0.06$ with standard errors $(0.03)$ (SI p. 41). The 2018 Correction identifies $-0.06$ as ‘the rounded covariate-adjusted estimated average treatment effect’ and $0.20$ as ‘the rounded unadjusted control group mean’, and gives 29% ‘without the rounding error’, 25% ‘using both covariate adjusted estimates’ and 23% ‘using both unadjusted estimates’. The relative reduction for estimated means $\hat\mu_0 > 0$ (control) and $\hat\mu_1$ (treatment) on a common basis is $(\hat\mu_0 - \hat\mu_1)/\hat\mu_0$. Rounding to a whole percent: $x$ rounds to 25% when $\tfrac{49}{200} \le x < \tfrac{51}{200}$ and to 30% when $\tfrac{59}{200} \le x < \tfrac{61}{200}$.
canonical_claim.note: P037-N001 is rated an error, Moderate (ratings.json). Sol's verdict is confirmed, by two validators, each upheld on re-run; evidence type recalculation_from_source, so there is no counterexample target. The error is already repaired by the official 2018 Correction; the target records the exact arithmetic that supports the corrected value from numbers printed in the original article. It is a finding about a reported number, included because the number is the abstract's headline figure, the correction changes a constant, and the supporting calculation is exact arithmetic on the paper's own totals. What a Lean proof can certify: (i)–(vi), which are comparisons of rational numbers. What it cannot certify: that the two totals are the model's unrounded predictions (they are the paper's estimates, taken as given), that the adjusted school-level ratio equals $\tfrac{683}{2695}$ exactly, or the Correction's 29% and 23%, which are the authors' statements and were not recomputed (the data file and analysis code are not staged). $\tfrac{1368}{5391}$ reduces to $\tfrac{152}{599}$. All comparisons were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, the display ‘The exposure mapping is:’, third line ($d_{NI}$), as printed: two feasible configurations that satisfy two cases at once (the validator's witnesses; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, SI p. 17] “The exposure mapping is:
$$f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = \begin{cases} d_C\ (\text{Control exposure}): & (1 - s_i) = 1\\ d_S\ (\text{School exposure}): & (1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0)s_i = 1\\ d_{NI}\ (\text{Non social referent seed exposure}): & \mathbf{I}((\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i = 0)s_i = 1\\ d_I\ (\text{Social referent seed exposure}): & (1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}((\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i > 0)s_i = 1\\ d_D\ (\text{Direct treatment condition}): & z_i = 1 \end{cases}$$”
[Witnesses.] Write $t_i = \mathbf{z}'\theta_i$ (the number of student $i$'s peers assigned to be seeds) and $r_i = (\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i$ (the number of student $i$'s referent peers assigned to be seeds), so that $s_i, z_i \in \{0,1\}$ and $t_i, r_i$ are integers with $0 \le r_i \le t_i$. The five printed conditions depend on $(s_i, z_i, t_i, r_i)$ only: C: $1 - s_i = 1$; S: $(1 - z_i)\,\mathbf{I}(t_i = 0)\,s_i = 1$; NI: $\mathbf{I}(r_i = 0)\,s_i = 1$; I: $(1 - z_i)\,\mathbf{I}(r_i > 0)\,s_i = 1$; D: $z_i = 1$.
(i) $(s_i, z_i, t_i, r_i) = (1, 0, 0, 0)$, a student in a treated school who is not a seed and none of whose peers is a seed, satisfies both S and NI.
(ii) $(s_i, z_i, t_i, r_i) = (1, 1, 0, 0)$, a seed none of whose peers is a seed, satisfies both NI and D.
(iii) In general every configuration that satisfies S satisfies NI (because $t_i = 0$ forces $r_i = 0$), and every configuration with $s_i = 1$, $z_i = 1$ and $r_i = 0$ satisfies both NI and D.
Hence the five printed cases do not define a function of $(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i)$: on these configurations two different exposures are assigned.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: SI p. 17: “An exposure mapping is a unit-specific function that maps an assignment vector, $\mathbf{z}$, and student-specific traits, $\theta_i$, to the actual exposure that a student receives. Each of the distinct exposures are allowed to give rise to distinct potential outcomes for each student. In this setting, exposure will refer to the student's proximity to referent seeds and nonreferent seeds (we will formalize this shortly). Define $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z},\theta_i)$ such that $\Pr(D_i = d) = \pi_i(d)$. We define the exposure mapping as a function, $f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i)$, such that the parameter, $\theta_i$, equals student $i$'s row in the network adjacency matrix. Further let $\gamma$ be an $N$-length vector denoting referent vs. nonreferent status, so that the $j$th element of $\gamma$ takes on the value 1 if student $j$ has an indegree in the top decile of student $j$'s school, and 0 otherwise. The crossproduct of $z_i$ and $\theta_i$, $\mathbf{z}'\theta_i$, is equal to the number of student $i$'s peers that are assigned to be seeds. Further $(\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i$ is equal to the number of student $i$'s referent peers that are assigned to be seeds. For convenience, denote $s_i$ as an indicator for whether student $i$'s school has been assigned to be treated.” $\mathbf{I}(\cdot)$ is the indicator function and $\circ$ the entrywise product. Since $\theta_i$ and $\gamma$ have entries in $\{0,1\}$, $0 \le r_i \le t_i$. The verbal definition, main p. 568 (PDF p. 3): “(i) students in control schools, (ii) students in treated schools for whom no peers are seeds, (iii) students in treated schools for whom at least one peer is a seed but no seed is a social referent, and (iv) students in treated schools for whom at least one peer is a social referent seed.” Feasibility under the design (validator): a treated school has 20 to 32 seeds and a student names at most 10 peers, so the seeds can all lie outside a student's peers, whether or not that student is a seed.
canonical_claim.note: P037-E002 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json). Sol's verdict is confirmed (batch validation); evidence type exact_counterexample; the two witnesses are evaluated in P037-B01/work/checks.py and checks-output.json. The display as printed has no final full stop. The intended categories are clear from the verbal definition on main p. 568, and no error in the implemented classification or in any estimate is established. The corrected mapping is P037-T8.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, the exposure mapping, corrected: with the repaired $d_{NI}$ condition the five cases partition the assignments generated by the design
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] The display is transcribed in P037-T7. [Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-E002), verbatim] “Replace the d_NI condition with $(1-z_i)\mathbf I(\mathbf z^\prime\theta_i>0)\mathbf I((\mathbf z\circ\gamma)^\prime\theta_i=0)s_i=1$. Replace “crossproduct of $z_i$ and $\theta_i$” with “crossproduct of $\mathbf z$ and $\theta_i$”.”
[Corrected mapping.]
$$f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = \begin{cases} d_C\ (\text{Control exposure}): & (1 - s_i) = 1\\ d_S\ (\text{School exposure}): & (1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0)s_i = 1\\ d_{NI}\ (\text{Non social referent seed exposure}): & (1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i > 0)\mathbf{I}((\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i = 0)s_i = 1\\ d_I\ (\text{Social referent seed exposure}): & (1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}((\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i > 0)s_i = 1\\ d_D\ (\text{Direct treatment condition}): & z_i = 1 \end{cases}$$
[Claim.] With $t_i = \mathbf{z}'\theta_i$ and $r_i = (\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i$: for all $s_i, z_i \in \{0,1\}$ with $z_i \le s_i$ (a seed is in a treated school) and all integers $0 \le r_i \le t_i$, exactly one of the five corrected conditions holds, namely: $d_C$ if $s_i = 0$; $d_D$ if $s_i = 1$ and $z_i = 1$; $d_S$ if $s_i = 1$, $z_i = 0$ and $t_i = 0$; $d_{NI}$ if $s_i = 1$, $z_i = 0$, $t_i > 0$ and $r_i = 0$; $d_I$ if $s_i = 1$, $z_i = 0$ and $r_i > 0$. So the corrected display defines a function on the assignments generated by the design, and its four cases $d_C, d_S, d_{NI}, d_I$ are the four conditions of exposure defined in words on main p. 568. On the witnesses of P037-T7 it gives $d_S$ at $(1,0,0,0)$ and $d_D$ at $(1,1,0,0)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P037-T7. The hypothesis $z_i \le s_i$ is the design: seeds are drawn only in treated schools (SI pp. 16–17, ‘half of schools are assigned to control schools with no seeds’); without it a configuration with $s_i = 0$ and $z_i = 1$ would satisfy both $d_C$ and $d_D$. The hypothesis $0 \le r_i \le t_i$ holds because $\gamma$ and $\theta_i$ have entries in $\{0,1\}$.
canonical_claim.note: Repair cost: none. Sol's corrected line (prior_correction.corrected_text): “$s_i(1-z_i)\mathbf 1\{\mathbf z^\prime\theta_i>0\}\mathbf 1\{(\mathbf z\circ\gamma)^\prime\theta_i=0\}=1$.” The second part of the repair, ‘crossproduct of $\mathbf{z}$ and $\theta_i$’ for ‘crossproduct of $z_i$ and $\theta_i$’, corrects a scalar printed for a vector in the prose; the formula $\mathbf{z}'\theta_i$ beside it is printed correctly, and it needs no statement of its own. The validator's script checks the partition on all 133 configurations with at most 10 peers; the claim above is for all $t_i$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, the simulated exposure probability $\hat\pi_i(d_k)$ (printed twice), corrected: the Monte Carlo frequency of the draws that induce exposure $d_k$
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix p. 18 and p. 14 (supplement PDF pp. 18 and 14)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, SI p. 18] “This vector tells us the probability of $i$ being subject to each of the possible exposures in $\{d_C, ..., d_D\}$, $\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\Omega}\mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$. Each component probability, $\pi_i(d_k)$, is, by definition, equal to the expected proportion of treatment assignments that induce exposure $d_k$ for student $i$. We can achieve an arbitrarily precise estimate of $\pi_i$ via simulated random assignments of $\mathbf{Z}$ according to the experimental design: $\hat\pi_i(d_k) = \mathbf{I}[\frac1J\sum_{\ell=1}^{J} f(\mathbf{z}^J,\theta_i) = d_k]$, where $J$ is the number of simulated random assignments, and $z^J$ denotes the $J$th simulated random assignment vector. Aronow [52] provides details on the rate of convergence of the estimated probabilities. In our study, we use $J = 10,000$ replicates of the administration of treatment assignments to estimate the $\pi_i(d_k)$ values.” [Printed, SI p. 14] The same expression, in the sentence “We achieve an arbitrarily precise estimate of $\pi_i$ via $J = 10,000$ simulated random assignments of $\mathbf{Z}$ according to the experimental design: $\hat\pi_i(d_k) = \mathbf{I}[\frac1J\sum_{\ell=1}^{J} f(\mathbf{z}^J,\theta_i) = d_k]$, where $J$ is the number of simulated random assignments, and $z^J$ denotes the $J$th simulated random assignment vector.”
[Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-E003), verbatim] “$\widehat\pi_i(d_k)=\frac1J\sum_{\ell=1}^{J}\mathbf I[f(\mathbf z^{\ell},\theta_i)=d_k]$ on both SI pp. 14 and 18.”
[Corrected formula.] $\hat\pi_i(d_k) = \dfrac1J\sum_{\ell=1}^{J}\mathbf{I}[f(\mathbf{z}^{\ell},\theta_i) = d_k]$, where $\mathbf{z}^{\ell}$ denotes the $\ell$th simulated random assignment vector.
[Mathematical content.] Let $\mathbf{Z}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{Z}^{(J)}$ be independent draws from the design (each with the law of $\mathbf{Z}$ on $\Omega$), fix a student $i$ and an exposure $d_k$, and put $X_\ell = \mathbf{I}[f(\mathbf{Z}^{(\ell)},\theta_i) = d_k]$ and $\pi = \pi_i(d_k)$.
(i) $\mathrm{E}[X_\ell] = \pi$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X_\ell) = \pi(1-\pi)$.
(ii) $\hat\pi_i(d_k) = \frac1J\sum_\ell X_\ell$ has $\mathrm{E}[\hat\pi_i(d_k)] = \pi$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\pi_i(d_k)) = \pi(1-\pi)/J \le \tfrac1{4J}$; hence $\Pr(|\hat\pi_i(d_k) - \pi| > \varepsilon) \le \tfrac1{4J\varepsilon^2}$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$, and the estimate becomes arbitrarily precise as $J \to \infty$.
(iii) [The printed expression is a different quantity.] The printed right-hand side takes only the values 0 and 1, and its summand does not depend on the index of summation: with exposures coded as numbers it equals $\mathbf{I}[f(\mathbf{z}^J,\theta_i) = d_k]$, the indicator of the last draw, for every $J$. The validator's example: $J = 2$, exposures of the two draws coded $0$ and $1$, target $d_k = 1$. The corrected frequency is $\tfrac12$; the printed expression is $\mathbf{I}[\tfrac12(1 + 1) = 1] = 1$; and the printed expression with only the superscript $J$ changed to $\ell$ is $\mathbf{I}[\tfrac12(0 + 1) = 1] = 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\Omega$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$ and the exact probability $\pi_i(d_k)$ (SI pp. 16 and 18; standing assumption (S5)); the exposure mapping $f$ (SI p. 17; P037-T7, corrected in P037-T8). The exposure labels $d_C, d_S, d_{NI}, d_I, d_D$ are categories, so the average printed inside the indicator is not defined without a numerical coding; the validator's example uses a coding only to show the algebra. ‘Independent draws from the design’ is the reading of ‘simulated random assignments of $\mathbf{Z}$ according to the experimental design’. In the printed sentences the superscript in the formula is on a bold $\mathbf{z}$ and the one in the following clause on an italic $z$.
canonical_claim.note: P037-E003 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json). Sol's verdict is confirmed (batch validation); evidence type complete_derivation, so the small example of (iii) is kept inside this target and there is no separate counterexample target; it is evaluated in P037-B01/work/checks.py. Repair cost: none. Sol's corrected text adds that the estimator has variance $\pi_i(d_k)(1-\pi_i(d_k))/J$ for independent design draws, which is (ii). The preceding exact definition of $\pi_i(d_k)$ and the words ‘expected proportion’ fix the intended meaning, and no error in the simulation that was run is established. The limit in (ii) is the only asymptotic remark and follows from the finite bound. The claim on SI p. 14 that $J = 10,000$ draws give an ‘arbitrarily precise’ estimate is finding P037-N021, a clarity note, and is not a target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, ‘Consistency and asymptotic normality directly follow ... given a growing sequence of independent schools of finite size, as holds by construction given our between-school randomization’: the treatment indicators of two schools in one block are dependent (the validator's computation; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix p. 19 (supplement PDF p. 19); the design is on SI p. 5 and in Fig. S1, SI p. 24
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, SI p. 19] “Consistency and asymptotic normality directly follow from the law of large numbers and a Lindeberg-type central limit theorem given a growing sequence of independent schools of finite size, as holds by construction given our between-school randomization.”
[Witness.] One block of four schools $A, B, C, D$; the set of treated schools is one of the six two-element subsets, each with probability $\tfrac16$; $T_j$ is the indicator that school $j$ is treated.
(i) $\mathrm{E}[T_A] = \mathrm{E}[T_B] = \tfrac12$ (three of the six allocations treat a given school).
(ii) $\mathrm{E}[T_AT_B] = \tfrac16 \ne \tfrac14 = \mathrm{E}[T_A]\,\mathrm{E}[T_B]$, so $\mathrm{Cov}(T_A, T_B) = -\tfrac1{12}$ and $T_A$, $T_B$ are not independent; the same holds for every pair of distinct schools of the block.
(iii) The control-exposure indicators $1 - T_j$ (a student has exposure $d_C$ exactly when $1 - s_i = 1$) have the same covariance, $\mathrm{Cov}(1 - T_A, 1 - T_B) = -\tfrac1{12}$.
(iv) [Without assuming equal probabilities.] For any joint law of $(T_A, T_B, T_C, T_D) \in \{0,1\}^4$ with $T_A + T_B + T_C + T_D = 2$ always and $\Pr(T_j = 1) = \tfrac12$ for each $j$: $\mathrm{Var}(\sum_jT_j) = 0$, whereas mutually independent indicators with these marginals would have $\mathrm{Var}(\sum_jT_j) = 4\cdot\tfrac14 = 1$; and $\sum_{j \ne k}\mathrm{Cov}(T_j, T_k) = -1$, so at least one pair has negative covariance.
(v) [Blocks are independent.] For two blocks randomized independently in this way, the 36 joint allocations each have probability $\tfrac1{36}$, the product of the two marginal probabilities, and the covariance of the treatment indicators of two schools in different blocks is $0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The design: SI p. 5, ‘Schools were assigned to blocks of four, and randomized to receive the treatment or not within these blocks’, with ‘a 50% chance of receiving the anti-conflict program’; Fig. S1 caption (SI p. 24), ‘Within each of the 14 school blocks, two schools were assigned to control ..., and two to treatment’ (standing assumption (S1)). $s_i$ is the indicator that student $i$'s school is treated and the control exposure $d_C$ is the case $(1 - s_i) = 1$ (SI p. 17; P037-T7). The sentence refuted is about the estimator $\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k)$ of the average potential outcomes (SI p. 19, transcribed in P037-T11). The paper does not say that the two treated schools of a block are chosen with equal probabilities over the six pairs; the validator takes that as the usual reading, and (iv) does not need it.
canonical_claim.note: P037-E004 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json). Sol's verdict is confirmed, upheld on re-run; evidence type exact_counterexample (P037-E004/v1/artifact/check.py enumerates the six allocations and the 36 allocations of two blocks). What a proof establishes: the independence of schools asserted ‘by construction’ is false under the stated design. What it does not establish (Sol): that the estimator is inconsistent or not asymptotically normal, or that any reported estimate, variance or $P$ value is wrong. The repaired justification is P037-T11.
